Sperm Donor Children

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.......donor conceived children looking for biological parent

Unique Selling Point:
Phenomenon few people know about -- enormous genetic families without precedent in modern society.


Summary:
With the advent of home DNA testing, troves of individuals are learning of a non-paternity event within their own families, that is, somebody who is donor conceived, through IVF. Alarming numbers of individuals discover that their mom or dad, grandfather or grandmother was not who they were reported to be.

The revelation or discovery of the NPE can have a life changing impact on the individual. In many cases, the individual welcomes learning their truths and finds the knowledge empowering. For others, it can be devastating and catapult the person into a complex psychological experience for which they are not prepared.

Many have discovered dozens of donor siblings, with one group approaching 200 members - enormous genetic families without precedent in modern society.


Further information:
With the advent of home DNA testing, troves of individuals are learning of a non-paternity event within their own families, that is, somebody who is donor conceived, through IVF. Alarming numbers of individuals discover that their mom or dad, grandfather or grandmother was not who they were reported to be.

The revelation or discovery of the NPE can have a life changing impact on the individual. In many cases, the individual welcomes learning their truths and finds the knowledge empowering. For others, it can be devastating and catapult the person into a complex psychological experience for which they are not prepared.

Thousands of Donor Conceived children have located siblings and many have also found their biological parent.


PROPOSAL
This is a post on a Facebook group:
“Calling all sperm donors who went to Witwatersrand Medical School...Your amazing biological children are looking for you. We don't want your money or to break up your family. We are looking for our simple birthright that was stolen from us with your anonymity. We want to know more about ourselves and our ancestors. We want to see where we got our devilish good looks, and our great sense of humor. Aren't you a little bit curious too? Are you a child or wife of a doctor that went to Wits in the 1970-80's? There is a good probability that your dad/husband donated sperm. There may be so many half-siblings out there. Hey, you may need a kidney one day! www.donors-of-wits-med.com

Thanks to mail-order DNA tests and a proliferation of online registries, people conceived with donated sperm and eggs are increasingly connecting with their genetic relatives, forming a growing community with complex relationships and unique concerns.

Many have discovered dozens of donor siblings, with one group approaching 200 members - enormous genetic families without precedent in modern society.

Because most donations are anonymous, the resulting children often find it almost impossible to obtain crucial information. Medical journals have documented cases in which clusters of offspring have found each other while seeking treatment for the same rare genetic disease. The news is full of nightmarish headlines about sperm donors who falsified their educational backgrounds, hid illnesses or turned out to be someone other than expected - such as a fertility clinic doctor.

In South Africa there is no regulation. And in the US there is also no regulation.

In America the lack of federal action has infuriated members of donor families such as Wendy Kramer, a Colorado woman who penned the FDA petition: "There is no government agency that wants to step in to regulate or oversee the business of creating human beings," said Kramer, whose son, Ryan, 28, has so far discovered 16 half siblings conceived with sperm from the same donor. "As wonderful as the connections are, there is an underbelly. . . . It has really revealed how this lack of regulation has had ramifications for real families."

Eighteen years ago, Kramer and Ryan founded what has since become the largest online site for the donor-conceived, the Donor Sibling Registry, or DSR. In simplest terms, the DSR is a matching site. People type in their donor number - an anonymous code assigned by the fertility clinic - and connect with others born from sperm or eggs from the same donor. It's all voluntary, and contact is achieved through mutual consent.

Today, the DSR has more than 60,000 members and has helped connect about 16,000 offspring with their half siblings or donors. As the site grows, so does the potential for new connections. Ryan has discovered five "new" sisters in just the past four months.

South Africa
The issue surfaced in South Africa in August last year when it was discovered that a fertility doctor Dr Tony Walker could have sired 300 children in the 1960’s when he used his own sperm. Fiona Darrough, a South African living in Australia discovered 4 siblings. However, they do not want to participate in the programme because of sibling pressure, etc.


SOUTH AFRICAN CASE STUDY, MAXENE STOLOFF

Three years ago, when I was 33 I received an email from someone claiming to be my half-sister… writes Maxene. We matched up as half-siblings on the DNA website 23andme. This was an absolute life-changing surprise! I submitted my DNA to 23andme to get a better idea of where my ancestry was from, as my parents had been very vague. I never imagined discovering what I discovered.

My first thoughts were that my dad cheated and that’s how I have this half-sister. But she said her parents confessed that they used a sperm donor to conceive her and her sister.

The story is that he was a medical student at the University of Witwatersrand (Wits) in the late ’70s / early 80s. That was or is common practice for male medical students to donate sperm. I asked my parents if I was donor conceived. And they finally confessed their Big Secret. The story matched up with my new sister’s. We were conceived at Park Lane Fertility Centre Johannesburg.

Over the last few years I discovered that the brother I grew up with is only a half-sibling with a different sperm donor father. And I discovered through AncestryDNA.com that my sister and I have another sister. Our donor dad has at least 3 biological daughters. (We are all the same age.) We grew up in the same area of Johannesburg, who knows we might have met each other before. The scary thing is, how many siblings do we have? Do we have brothers we grew up with? Went to school with? Dated? Having an anonymous biological father/sibling could be dangerous. What happens if we marry (unbeknownst to us) our half-siblings?

Adopted children are supported and pushed to find and meet their biological parents. Why are donor-conceived children shunned of that same right? I’ve been giving my (amazing) social father’s medical history when asked. I feel so silly. They didn’t do genetic testing on sperm donations in the 80s. I am clueless on anything medical related on my father’s side.

I think these men are thoughtless and selfish going into sperm donation under anonymity.
I don’t know if they got paid back then, or if they had limits on how many times they could donate.

Who knows how many siblings I have? 5, 20, 400?

I live in the US now, my sisters both live in London. In the US, there is no regulation on sperm donation. I have recently discovered that I have another sibling in Germany.

In small communities there is a good incidence of a phenomenon called Genetic Sexual Attraction. This is where biological related strangers, have such a connection to each other – that they end up in an intimate relationship, only to find out they are close relatives. (As seen on ‘Sisters’ on Netflix.) I’m 100% sure that sperm donation was or is taking place at universities all around SA and the world. Parents want their children’s seed to come from someone “intelligent”, so finding a college-educated donor is very popular.

I’m not trying to wreck my biological father’s family, and I don’t want money from him. At the very least I would like a full medical history. (And perhaps a photo

Script:


V/O:
The Big Apple. New York is home to 8 million people, one of them is 36-year-old, South African-born, Maxene Stoloff. About 5 years ago Stoloff did what over 30-million Americans have done: using a mail-order DNA kit to submit her DNA for analysis.
Maxene:
Everyone is doing it, and I love to give them out as Christmas and Birthday presents, because they are like a perfect little gift.
V/O:
Stoloff submitted the results to a number of websites that compare millions of profiles worldwide with one other and identify related profiles. She did it, at best hoping to discover a distant relative.

South Africans can also order these tests from abroad, take buccal swabs or saliva, and send the samples back to the company of origin for testing.
LINK:
This is a mail-in kit from Australia. It comes with the instructions, and this is where you put in the saliva sample. You put in into this box, seal it in this plastic over here, you send it over, and in a couple of months, you get your results.
V/O:
After Stoloff submitted her profile to a number of DNA-matching sites, she happened to be travelling in India, when she got information that turned her world upside-down.
Maxene: and I got an e-mail and the title of the e-mail was “Hallo, I am your sister”.
Maxene: I was in a daze and so I e-mailed back and I said: “I always wanted a sister”.
V/O:
Despite her humorous response, far away from home, Stoloff was stunned. She had more questions than answers.
Maxene:
I did not quite understand like how this was. Why was my dad, why would he be her dad as well. Did he have an affair? What is going on there.
V/O:
Growing up in London, Stoloff’s half-sister had the answer – her mother had told her that she was donor-conceived. This meant that Stoloff too, was donor-conceived – a fact her mother then confirmed. But it was not the end of the roller-coaster ride for her.
Maxene:
And yes, about 2 years after I found Sasha I was just sitting in central Park looking at my phone, and I get a text message from Sasha saying” Hey, we have a new sister!”
V/O:
Their new-found sister was also from London. Stoloff went to meet the two of them. About two months ago they discovered yet another sister living in Germany. Stoloff’s sisters chose not reveal their identities.
Maxene:
I beieve two of the sister’s dads don’t know that they know.
V/O:
So, there in New York she went from being an only daughter, to one of at least four sisters, and with a father she knew nothing about.

Stoloff’s case is not unique. In the US, where DNA testing is common, donor-conceived children have been discovering siblings and donor fathers they never knew they had.

The phenomenon has brought about extraordinary genetic families. For example, here Peter Ellensteen of Los Angeles meets two daughters he never knew he had, at the airport.

But soon they were joined by another 23 siblings. Decades ago, Ellenstein donated sperm to a sperm bank and at least 25 children were conceived. As DNA profiling grows, huge genetic families are increasingly being discovered.

Keen to identify her biological father, Maxene Stoloff put a call out on Facebook to try and find other South African donor-conceived children. She and her half-sisters figured out that they had been conceived in Johannesburg, from the sperm of a Wits medical student in the 1990s.

Rani Pillay, a law lecturer at the University of Pretoria specialises in Medical Law and Bio-ethics.
Question:
And what does legislation currently say about the rights of donor conceived children.
Rani:
So currently South African law does not allow the identity of the gamete donor to be released to the child.
V/O:
Under the law, as it stands, only limited information about a donor can be disclosed. Mandy Rodriques is a clinical psychologist who counsels donors and recipients at Medfem Fertility Clinic.
Mandy:
So with sperm donor you are looking at the general features – complexion, race, you get a column with height, hair colour, eye colour, hobbies , education. It is very limited.
V/O:
Esmeralda Butterworth, a donor-conceived child from Cape Town feels donor anonymity should be abolished.
Esmeralda:
Secrecy is harmful and donor conceived people need to know their identity or understand their identity. I got sick three years ago and it came to appoint where they said well, we are going to have to back to Mom’s medical history and then of course, your dad’s. And when they asked me that I could not answer that.
V/O:
Butterworth feels that, like adopted children, who are allowed to discover the identity of biological parents, donor-conceived children should be allowed the same – a sentiment Stoloff echoes.
Maxene:
Why don’t we have the same rights to find our biological family.
V/O:
Stoloff and Butterworth are not alone in their demand.
Mandy:
There is this whole movement around the world now that children have a right to know the identity and they need closure, and that is where the world is moving. There are slowly making known donors the norm and I think it is coming to South Africa.
V/O:
For the time being, donor anonymity here is still protected, but with 12 live births allowed per sperm donor, and no way of monitoring and limiting such births, a South African sperm donor could literally father dozens of offspring.

Another such large genetic family in the US is that of sperm donor Michael Rubino who sired no less than 19 children. They also discovered one another through DNA profiles.

Huge genetic families are sure to exist here as well, but they have not yet been identified, because so few South Africans have DNA profiles online. But it is likely on its way and therefore issues around donor anonymity will increasingly have to be re-examined.
LINK:
It seems that the challenge in South Africa is a balancing act between the rights of the donor conceived child and the rights of the gamete donor.
V/O:
Abolishing sperm donor anonymity may be on the cards here.
Question:
Won’t it deter some people?
Rani:
It might deter some people, but studies have show in other juris dictions where donor anonymity has been abolished that the pool of donors has initially declined and thereafter and picked up and what needs to be remembered is that there is no legal relationship between a gamete donor and the child that he has contributed to in terms of genetic material. The law only recognizes a relationship between the commissioning parents, the donor recipients, and the child. The child has no parent child relationship with the donor and can have no expectation of a right to inheritance or maintenance for that matter.
V/O:
Even though she has lived in the US for 26 years, Maxene Stoloff is very keen to meet her donor father. But her search so far has led nowhere………. And Esmeralda Butterworth dreams of meeting her biological father too.
Question:
What would you say to him?
Esmeralda:
I think I would hug him and just look at his face and see if we look alike. Mainly I would just say thank your for giving me the opportunity to live and that he blessed my parents with a child because I know it was their biggest dream.

Mandy: So with sperm donor you are looking at the general features – complexion, race, you get a column with height, hair colour, eye colour, hobbies , education. It is very limited. V/O: Esmeralda Butterworth, a donor-conceived child from Cape Town feels donor anonymity should be abolished. Esmeralda: Secrecy is harmful and donor conceived people need to know their identity or understand their identity. I got sick three years ago and it came to appoint where they said well, we are going to have to back to Mom’s medical history and then of course, your dad’s. And when they asked me that I could not answer that. V/O: Butterworth feels that, like adopted children, who are allowed to discover the identity of biological parents, donor-conceived children should be allowed the same – a sentiment Stoloff echoes. Maxene: Why don’t we have the same rights to find our biological family. V/O: Stoloff and Butterworth are not alone in their demand. Mandy: There is this whole movement around the world now that children have a right to know the identity and they need closure, and that is where the world is moving. There are slowly making known donors the norm and I think it is coming to South Africa. V/O: For the time being, donor anonymity here is still protected, but with 12 live births allowed per sperm donor, and no way of monitoring and limiting such births, a South African sperm donor could literally father dozens of offspring. Another such large genetic family in the US is that of sperm donor Michael Rubino who sired no less than 19 children. They also discovered one another through DNA profiles. Huge genetic families are sure to exist here as well, but they have not yet been identified, because so few South Africans have DNA profiles online. But it is likely on its way and therefore issues around donor anonymity will increasingly have to be re-examined. LINK: It seems that the challenge in South Africa is a balancing act between the rights of the donor conceived child and the rights of the gamete donor. V/O: Abolishing sperm donor anonymity may be on the cards here. Question: Won’t it deter some people? Rani: It might deter some people, but studies have show in other juris dictions where donor anonymity has been abolished that the pool of donors has initially declined and thereafter and picked up and what needs to be remembered is that there is no legal relationship between a gamete donor and the child that he has contributed to in terms of genetic material. The law only recognizes a relationship between the commissioning parents, the donor recipients, and the child. The child has no parent child relationship with the donor and can have no expectation of a right to inheritance or maintenance for that matter. V/O: Even though she has lived in the US for 26 years, Maxene Stoloff is very keen to meet her donor father. But her search so far has led nowhere………. And Esmeralda Butterworth dreams of meeting her biological father too. Question: What would you say to him? Esmeralda: I think I would hug him and just look at his face and see if we look alike. Mainly I would just say thank your for giving me the opportunity to live and that he blessed my parents with a child because I know it was their biggest dream.

metadata.Summary: With the advent of home DNA testing, troves of individuals are learning of a non-paternity event within their own families, that is, somebody who is donor conceived, through IVF. Alarming numbers of individuals discover that their mom or dad, grandfather or grandmother was not who they were reported to be. The revelation or discovery of the NPE can have a life changing impact on the individual. In many cases, the individual welcomes learning their truths and finds the knowledge empowering. For others, it can be devastating and catapult the person into a complex psychological experience for which they are not prepared. Many have discovered dozens of donor siblings, with one group approaching 200 members - enormous genetic families without precedent in modern society.

Thousands of Donor Conceived children have located siblings and many have also found their biological parent. PROPOSAL This is a post on a Facebook group: “Calling all sperm donors who went to Witwatersrand Medical School...Your amazing biological children are looking for you. We don't want your money or to break up your family. We are looking for our simple birthright that was stolen from us with your anonymity. We want to know more about ourselves and our ancestors. We want to see where we got our devilish good looks, and our great sense of humor. Aren't you a little bit curious too? Are you a child or wife of a doctor that went to Wits in the 1970-80's? There is a good probability that your dad/husband donated sperm. There may be so many half-siblings out there. Hey, you may need a kidney one day! www.donors-of-wits-med.com Thanks to mail-order DNA tests and a proliferation of online registries, people conceived with donated sperm and eggs are increasingly connecting with their genetic relatives, forming a growing community with complex relationships and unique concerns. Many have discovered dozens of donor siblings, with one group approaching 200 members - enormous genetic families without precedent in modern society. Because most donations are anonymous, the resulting children often find it almost impossible to obtain crucial information. Medical journals have documented cases in which clusters of offspring have found each other while seeking treatment for the same rare genetic disease. The news is full of nightmarish headlines about sperm donors who falsified their educational backgrounds, hid illnesses or turned out to be someone other than expected - such as a fertility clinic doctor. In South Africa there is no regulation. And in the US there is also no regulation. In America the lack of federal action has infuriated members of donor families such as Wendy Kramer, a Colorado woman who penned the FDA petition: "There is no government agency that wants to step in to regulate or oversee the business of creating human beings," said Kramer, whose son, Ryan, 28, has so far discovered 16 half siblings conceived with sperm from the same donor. "As wonderful as the connections are, there is an underbelly. . . . It has really revealed how this lack of regulation has had ramifications for real families." Eighteen years ago, Kramer and Ryan founded what has since become the largest online site for the donor-conceived, the Donor Sibling Registry, or DSR. In simplest terms, the DSR is a matching site. People type in their donor number - an anonymous code assigned by the fertility clinic - and connect with others born from sperm or eggs from the same donor. It's all voluntary, and contact is achieved through mutual consent. Today, the DSR has more than 60,000 members and has helped connect about 16,000 offspring with their half siblings or donors. As the site grows, so does the potential for new connections. Ryan has discovered five "new" sisters in just the past four months. South Africa The issue surfaced in South Africa in August last year when it was discovered that a fertility doctor Dr Tony Walker could have sired 300 children in the 1960’s when he used his own sperm. Fiona Darrough, a South African living in Australia discovered 4 siblings. However, they do not want to participate in the programme because of sibling pressure, etc. SOUTH AFRICAN CASE STUDY, MAXENE STOLOFF Three years ago, when I was 33 I received an email from someone claiming to be my half-sister… writes Maxene. We matched up as half-siblings on the DNA website 23andme. This was an absolute life-changing surprise! I submitted my DNA to 23andme to get a better idea of where my ancestry was from, as my parents had been very vague. I never imagined discovering what I discovered. My first thoughts were that my dad cheated and that’s how I have this half-sister. But she said her parents confessed that they used a sperm donor to conceive her and her sister. The story is that he was a medical student at the University of Witwatersrand (Wits) in the late ’70s / early 80s. That was or is common practice for male medical students to donate sperm. I asked my parents if I was donor conceived. And they finally confessed their Big Secret. The story matched up with my new sister’s. We were conceived at Park Lane Fertility Centre Johannesburg. Over the last few years I discovered that the brother I grew up with is only a half-sibling with a different sperm donor father. And I discovered through AncestryDNA.com that my sister and I have another sister. Our donor dad has at least 3 biological daughters. (We are all the same age.) We grew up in the same area of Johannesburg, who knows we might have met each other before. The scary thing is, how many siblings do we have? Do we have brothers we grew up with? Went to school with? Dated? Having an anonymous biological father/sibling could be dangerous. What happens if we marry (unbeknownst to us) our half-siblings? Adopted children are supported and pushed to find and meet their biological parents. Why are donor-conceived children shunned of that same right? I’ve been giving my (amazing) social father’s medical history when asked. I feel so silly. They didn’t do genetic testing on sperm donations in the 80s. I am clueless on anything medical related on my father’s side. I think these men are thoughtless and selfish going into sperm donation under anonymity. I don’t know if they got paid back then, or if they had limits on how many times they could donate. Who knows how many siblings I have? 5, 20, 400? I live in the US now, my sisters both live in London. In the US, there is no regulation on sperm donation. I have recently discovered that I have another sibling in Germany. In small communities there is a good incidence of a phenomenon called Genetic Sexual Attraction. This is where biological related strangers, have such a connection to each other – that they end up in an intimate relationship, only to find out they are close relatives. (As seen on ‘Sisters’ on Netflix.) I’m 100% sure that sperm donation was or is taking place at universities all around SA and the world. Parents want their children’s seed to come from someone “intelligent”, so finding a college-educated donor is very popular.
